stories.title: Dongbei Chinese Restaurant & Bar Inks Deal at 63 Cooper Square
stories.excerpt: Dongbei Chinese Restaurant & Bar is opening its fourth location in New York City and its fifth overall, Commercial Observer has learned. The growing Northern Chinese dining concept signed a 2,000-square-foot lease at 63 Cooper Square, an East Village property owned by Matthew Rettner, according to landlord broker Meridian Capital Group. Asking rent for the space was $21,600 per month, and the tenant signed a 15-year lease. The midblock site is one of several small commercial spots on the ground floor of a residential building along Third Avenue between St. Marks Place and East Seventh Street. “Cooper Square doesn’t have a ton of turnover, so when a turnkey restaurant space becomes available there, we want a tenant who can hit the ground running,” Meridian’s Daniel Zacaim said in a statement. “Dongbei’s operating history made this an easy recommendation to the landlord, and I think this location is going to perform very well for them.” Zacaim represented the landlord alongside Noam Aziz and Carson Shahrabani, while David Green and Benjamin Namdar of KSR negotiated on behalf of the tenant. The KSR brokers did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “What’s impressive about Dongbei is the consistency of their growth — four locations in New York plus a New Jersey expansion in the works,” Shahrabani said in a statement. “That kind of momentum makes landlords comfortable, and it made this negotiation move quickly and smoothly on both sides.” Dongbei has Manhattan locations at 953 Columbus Avenue on the Upper West Side, 367 West 36th Street in Midtown and 17 Ann Street in the Financial District, as well as a spot in Downtown Jersey City. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Dongbei Chinese Restaurant signed 2,000-sf lease at 63 Cooper Square, East Village Manhattan.
15-year lease at $21,600/month ($129.60/sf annually) signals ground-floor retail stability.
Limited turnover in Cooper Square suggests strong residential anchoring, minimal disruption.
stories.summary: Dongbei Chinese Restaurant & Bar leased 2,000 square feet at 63 Cooper Square in the East Village for $21,600 per month on a 15-year deal. The tenant, expanding to its fifth location, chose a turnkey space in a residential building along Third Avenue. The broker noted low turnover in the Cooper Square submarket and confidence in the tenant's operating history.
stories.impact: Minimal direct relevance to multifamily development. Ground-floor retail demand in East Village reflects healthy mixed-use fundamentals in established residential neighborhoods, but this single lease does not signal new apartment demand drivers or supply pressures in Manhattan.

stories.title: Power Is No Longer an Input in Data Centers. It Is the Product.
stories.excerpt: A data center site can have land, fiber, approvals and a customer ready to deploy, and still be nearly worthless. The reason is changing what developers are actually searching for. Power scarcity is changing the economics of development. On power grid operator PJM, capacity prices jumped from $28.92 per megawatt-day for 2024-2025 to $269.92 for 2025-2026, then climbed again to $329.17 for 2026-2027. Power availability is increasingly becoming the asset around which everything else is assembled. Suhail Y Tayeb. PHOTO: Courtesy NYU Land and fiber still matter. But neither creates a viable project if electricity cannot arrive when the customer needs it. That changes the site-selection conversation. Where is the substation? How much capacity is actually available? When can the first tranche of power be delivered? A hyperscaler may ultimately need hundreds of megawatts, but not all on day one. If 50 megawatts can be energized now and another 100 can arrive 18 months later, that site may be more valuable than one promising 300 megawatts several years from now. Power is not valuable simply because it exists on a utility map. It is valuable when it can be delivered. That distinction is forcing developers deeper into the energy business. They are pursuing utility relationships, transmission access, substations and gas infrastructure with the same intensity they once reserved for land and entitlements. They are also confronting a mismatch in timelines. AI companies plan deployments in months. Major transmission projects, substations and generation assets can take much longer. The result is a growing market for solutions that bridge the gap. Behind-the-meter generation, co-generation and direct energy partnerships are increasingly part of the conversation. The question is no longer simply whether a utility can serve a project, but whether and how the developer can assemble an energy system until the grid catches up. bullets: PJM capacity prices surged $28.92 (2024-25) to $329.17/MW-day (2026-27) — 11x increase.
Power availability now primary site-selection constraint; land and fiber insufficient without grid capacity.
Developers shifting to phased power delivery models to unlock feasible data center projects today.
stories.summary: Power capacity prices on PJM grid operator have exploded from $28.92 per megawatt-day in 2024-2025 to $329.17 in 2026-2027, forcing data center developers to prioritize electricity availability over traditional site attributes. Land, fiber, and entitlements no longer create viable projects without confirmed, near-term power delivery. Developers now compete on ability to access partial capacity upfront and phase deployments rather than securing full capacity years out.
stories.impact: This fundamentally reshapes site selection logic across major multifamily markets reliant on hyperscaler growth (Northern Virginia, Austin, Phoenix, Northern New Jersey). Data center demand—a key employment and tax base driver for residential development—is now constrained by grid capacity bottlenecks, not land scarcity. Developers competing for land near data center clusters may face higher acquisition costs and extended timelines as power availability becomes the binding constraint, delaying ancillary housing absorption and forcing rents higher in already-tight markets.

stories.title: Anthony Cohen of Northmarq: 5 Questions
stories.excerpt: Northmarq’s Anthony Cohen is six years into his commercial real estate career and already holds top roles at a firm noted for its leasing, sales and debt acumen. Cohen, 34, is a managing director in Northmarq’s Los Angeles commercial investment sales office and co-leader of the firm’s national net-lease and sale-leaseback group. Since 2020 — when he started his real estate brokerage career at Ascension — Cohen has worked on deals with a cumulative volume exceeding $1 billion. His experience in both real estate and finance — he worked at J.P. Morgan for two years after college — make him a pro at advising businesses on their real estate needs. Cohen, who leads a team of five producers at Northmarq, said the most popular investment today is one that saves buyers money on taxes: accelerated depreciated assets like gas stations, car washes or even oil change sites. “Those are the most interesting and most highly sought-after assets right now,” he said. Commercial Observer sat down with Cohen last week to discuss that investment trend, his career so far, and what he’s seeing in the market today. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: Walk me through how you got started in real estate and where you were before Northmarq. Anthony Cohen: So I’m not too young, but not too old. I went to Penn State. I studied finance. My first job was at J.P. Morgan. I was working just outside of Philadelphia in Delaware, actually, and I was a financial analyst there, and, you know, did really well. Even though I got all the accolades of being a high performer, it’s very corporate, and upward mobility compensation is very hard to change. You just have to put in the hours and the years, and you’ll eventually be moving up the ladder. It was a really good experience to learn how to become a professional in the outside world, but I wanted something that had unlimited potential. Cohen notes accelerated depreciation assets—gas stations, car washes, oil change sites—are the most highly sought investment products today due to tax benefits. The profile does not provide market-level metrics or forward guidance.

stories.title: Sunday Summary: Sharp Left
stories.excerpt: Summer’s done, and the hustle of fall will soon be upon us. Part of the background noise of the season will be the elections for state and federal legislatures. That includes the New York State Senate and Assembly. Those august Albany chambers are about to absorb a relatively large number of Democratic Socialists — and their allies — in the same vein as New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. That could have serious ramifications for commercial real estate. We’re talking retail rent control; further restrictions on raising the rent on, or vacating, rent-stabilized apartments; and a much longer moratorium on the development of large-scale data centers. There’s also some potential good news in so many far-left pols heading up the Hudson at once: They have aggressive plans for fostering the development of much-needed affordable housing. Those plans should align with the commercial real estate industry’s own efforts (really). Otherwise, though, next year could bring regressive changes akin to the dreaded 2019 state housing legislation that followed lefty wins in the 2018 elections. Options can be a lifesaver Speaking of affordable housing, a niche financing option for the asset class is growing in popularity. It’s called tax-exempt commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) debt. That debt can carry lower costs of capital than standard taxable CMBS or the affordable housing loans that Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac back. (For more on the state of CMBS, check out our Q&A with Trepp’s Stephen Buschbom and Andy Boettcher.) And, apropos of both legislatures and affordable housing, there’s a lot to recommend for the CRE industry in the recently enacted 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. It’s the biggest single piece of federal housing legislation in decades, and it’s meant to foster a lot of new housing construction, particularly of the subsidized sort. Will it? bullets: NY State Senate/Assembly races expected to gain Democratic Socialists, allies of Mayor Mamdani.
Policy risks: retail rent control, stricter rent-stabilized restrictions, data center development moratorium.
Offsetting upside: aggressive affordable housing development plans may align with industry priorities.
stories.summary: Democratic Socialist and progressive candidates aligned with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani are expected to win multiple New York State Senate and Assembly seats in the fall elections. Their policy agenda includes retail rent control, tighter restrictions on rent-stabilized apartment rent increases and vacancies, and an extended data center development moratorium, though they also support accelerated affordable housing development.
stories.impact: HIGH RISK TO NEW YORK MULTIFAMILY DEVELOPMENT. Rent-stabilized expansion or stricter de-stabilization rules would compress value on existing portfolios and suppress new market-rate development feasibility in Manhattan and outer boroughs. Data center moratorium delays tech job concentration and population influx. However, if affordable housing incentives include density bonuses, tax abatements (PILOT), or expedited permitting, TCR should monitor for entitlement opportunities in Bronx, Brooklyn, Queens submarkets tied to affordable-housing overlays.

stories.title: Global Holdings Lands $382M Refi for Midtown Tower
stories.excerpt: Private equity firm Global Holdings has secured a $382.4 million refinancing loan for its Midtown Manhattan office tower at 120 Park Ave., with Wells Fargo and German bank LBBW originating the note. The funding, reported by The Real Deal, retires the property’s existing $335 million loan from HSBC. The recapitalization follows Bloomberg LP’s renewal in late 2025 of its 495,753-square-foot lease across 20 floors of the Class A building, marking one of the city’s largest lease deals of the year. Bloomberg’s lease, which was extended to 2024, accounts for roughly 80% of the property’s rentable area. Global Holdings acquired the 620,000-square-foot building neighboring Grand Central Terminal from Altria Group in 2008. The refinancing will facilitate a capital improvement program for the asset, which was built in 1981. Chaired by Eyal Ofer, Global Holdings has an international real estate portfolio spanning more than 10 million square feet of real estate, including 120 properties and over 1,500 hotel rooms. The post Global Holdings Lands $382M Refi for Midtown Tower appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Global Holdings refinanced 120 Park Ave. (Midtown Manhattan) with $382.4M from Wells Fargo, LBBW.
Bloomberg LP renewed 495,753-sf lease (20 floors, 80% of building) to 2024; one of year's largest deals.
Class A office refinancing signals persistent tenant demand in Grand Central submarket despite market headwinds.
stories.summary: Global Holdings secured a $382.4 million refinancing from Wells Fargo and German lender LBBW for 120 Park Ave., a 620,000-square-foot Midtown Manhattan office tower built in 1981. The deal was triggered by Bloomberg LP's late-2025 lease renewal for 495,753 square feet across 20 floors—80% of the building—one of the city's largest office leases this year. The refi will fund capital improvements.
stories.impact: Moderate indirect signal for Manhattan multifamily. Bloomberg's large lease renewal in Class A Midtown office (Grand Central submarket) indicates sustained employer demand and employment stability in core Manhattan, supporting residential absorption in nearby neighborhoods. However, office-to-residential conversion plays remain contingent on broader office market deterioration; this strong renewal suggests conversion pressure remains limited in Midtown proper, but may redirect residential demand to outer-borough tech/startup clusters and Midtown South.

stories.title: NYC Plans 215-Unit Bronx Apartment Building
stories.excerpt: New York City’s Department of Housing Preservation & Development (HPD) has filed plans for a 215-unit apartment building on a vacant city-owned lot in the Bronx’s Melrose neighborhood. The 176,000-square-foot building at 3116–3124 Third Ave. would rise 20 stories, the New York Business Journal reported, citing plans filed with the New York City Planning Commission. HPD revealed that it has chosen Bronx-based developer Procida Cos. and community development nonprofit Nos Quedamos for the project. The building would also come with 7,000 square feet of commercial space and amenities including a community room, second-floor terrace and roof terrace. If realized, the project would advance the Melrose Commons Urban Renewal Plan, which proposes to bring new affordable housing across a 33-block area. To make way for the project, HPD is requesting that the city remove the 85-foot height limit for new multifamily developments in the vicinity. The department has also asked the Planning Commission create an Urban Development Action Area Program within the neighborhood that would set forth guidelines for developing income-restricted and affordable housing. The post NYC Plans 215-Unit Bronx Apartment Building appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NYC HPD filing 215-unit affordable building at 3116-3124 Third Ave., Bronx Melrose neighborhood.
20-story, 176,000-sf project with 7,000-sf retail; requests 85-foot height limit removal.
Part of Melrose Commons Urban Renewal Plan (33-block affordable housing initiative).
stories.summary: New York City's HPD has filed plans for a 215-unit affordable apartment building in the Bronx's Melrose neighborhood on a city-owned lot. The 176,000-square-foot, 20-story building at 3116-3124 Third Avenue will include 7,000 square feet of ground-floor retail and mixed amenities. Developer Procida Cos. and community nonprofit Nos Quedamos are the selected partners. HPD is requesting removal of the 85-foot height limit to enable the project and creation of an Urban Development Action Area to facilitate affordable-housing-focused development across the 33-block Melrose Commons area.
stories.impact: POSITIVE SIGNAL FOR BRONX MULTIFAMILY DEMAND AND REGULATORY ENVIRONMENT. HPD's public commitment to 215 units plus zoning relief (height-limit waiver, UDAA creation) demonstrates political will for density and housing supply in Melrose. This lowers regulatory risk for private developers pursuing adjacent or similar-scale projects. However, public-sector development timeline is typically 3-5 years; private market players should monitor zoning changes and tax-incentive structures (PILOT, 421-a successors) to deploy capital in Melrose and nearby Third Avenue corridors ahead of HPD completion, capturing upside from population stabilization and infrastructure investment.

stories.title: Northern New Jersey Shopping Center Changes Hands
stories.excerpt: Adoni Property Group has acquired the 60,614-square-foot shopping center in Northern New Jersey’s Basking Ridge from Kushner Real Estate Group. JLL Capital Markets arranged the sale and secured $12.2 million in acquisition financing on behalf of the buyer through an unidentified life insurance firm. Built in 2000, the community retail center spans approximately 11 acres at 546 Allen Rd. and includes five buildings that were fully leased to 18 tenants at the time of the sale. Four new leases executed within the past 12 months point to continued momentum at the property. Anchored by Walgreens and United States Postal Service locations, the shopping center sits within the master-planned community The Hills at Basking Ridge. “Highlands Village is a premier, necessity-based retail center with a proven history of stability and long-term tenant loyalty,” said Sonny Adoni, founder and CEO of Adoni Property Group in a statement. Westfield, NJ-based Adoni develops and manages a diversified portfolio of residential and commercial properties. Headquartered in Jersey City, Kushner Real Estate Group is a real estate investment and management firm with a portfolio of apartments and commercial space across four states. The post Northern New Jersey Shopping Center Changes Hands appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Adoni Property Group acquired Basking Ridge (NJ) shopping center from Kushner for undisclosed price.
60,614-sf center (11 acres) built 2000, 18 tenants fully leased; 4 new leases in past 12 months.
Necessity-based retail (Walgreens, USPS anchor) within master-planned residential community.
stories.summary: Adoni Property Group purchased a 60,614-square-foot shopping center in Basking Ridge, Northern New Jersey from Kushner Real Estate Group, with $12.2 million in acquisition financing secured through an insurance lender. Built in 2000, the 11-acre property spans five buildings with 18 tenants and achieved full occupancy at sale. Walgreens and USPS anchor the center, which sits within the master-planned residential community The Hills at Basking Ridge.
stories.impact: Indirect positive for Northern New Jersey multifamily. Necessity-based retail stabilization and new leasing activity (4 in past 12 months) in master-planned community signals ongoing residential demand absorption in Basking Ridge submarket. Retail transaction validates underlying population and household formation; multifamily developers should monitor for opportunities in same or adjacent phases of The Hills, or other master-planned communities in Northern Jersey suburbs benefiting from NYC-commuter demand and stable household formation.

stories.title: Iconic Rancho Cordova Furniture Showroom Listed for Sale
stories.excerpt: The longtime Rancho Cordova showroom of Beck’s Furniture has been listed for sale. The 208,800-square-foot property at 11840 Folsom Blvd has served primarily as a warehouse and distribution center for Beck’s Furniture, where people came to view the chairs and sofas before buying. The company closed its doors last year. The 10 acres along the Highway 50 corridor and has served as one of Northern California’s most recognizable furniture destinations for nearly 50 years. It features an approximately 90,000 square feet of showroom space and 120,000 square feet of warehouse and distribution space. Morrow Botros, Bryce MacDonald and Jay Hamer of Cushman & Wakefield have been exclusively retained to market the asset on behalf of the seller, Beck’s Furniture & Sleep / Beckinger Family Ownership.  Botros added, “For nearly 50 years, the Beck’s Furniture campus has stood as one of the Sacramento region’s most recognizable commercial landmarks. Few properties can claim both institutional scale and deep community recognition.” The post Iconic Rancho Cordova Furniture Showroom Listed for Sale appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Beck's Furniture Rancho Cordova showroom (208,800-sf, 10 acres) listed for sale; company closed 2024.
90,000-sf showroom + 120,000-sf warehouse/distribution on Highway 50 corridor.
50-year-old landmark property; no development or user change announced.
stories.summary: The longtime Beck's Furniture showroom in Rancho Cordova, California has been listed for sale following the company's closure in 2024. The 208,800-square-foot property spans 10 acres along Highway 50 and includes approximately 90,000 square feet of showroom space and 120,000 square feet of warehouse/distribution facilities. Cushman & Wakefield is marketing the asset for the Beckinger family.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. Large warehouse/showroom conversion opportunity exists on Highway 50 corridor (Sacramento exurban), but no adaptive-use or redevelopment plans announced. If site is repositioned for industrial, logistics, or flex-office use, could signal positive activity in Rancho Cordova employment market; multifamily developers should flag Highway 50 corridor for future demand catalysts if new industrial or distribution tenants anchor the site.

stories.title: Tishman Speyer Trades Mountain View Office Building for $121.5M
stories.excerpt: Tishman Speyer sold 400 Castro Street, a 100 percent leased, Class A office building in downtown Mountain View, California. Spear Street Capital was the buyer in the $121.5 million transaction. Tishman Speyer developed the 138,000-square-foot property in 2002 and immediately leased the office space in full to Fenwick & West, which has remained a customer in the building. Tishman Speyer claims the transaction represents one of the strongest pricing outcomes for a Mountain View office sale in recent years. Centrally located with convenient access to highways and Caltrain, 400 Castro features expansive roof decks, underground parking and views of the San Francisco Bay and coastal mountains. The property, which was 100% leased at the time of the sale, is located in the heart of Downtown Mountain View, surrounded by restaurants and retail, with Cascal restaurant, Peet’s Coffee, and Sweetgreen on site. Tishman Speyer was represented by the Eastdil Secured team led by Nate Jones. The post Tishman Speyer Trades Mountain View Office Building for $121.5M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Tishman Speyer sold 400 Castro Street (Mountain View) to Spear Street Capital for $121.5M.
138,000-sf Class A office, 100% leased to Fenwick & West law firm since 2002 development.
Described as 'one of strongest pricing outcomes' for Mountain View office in recent years.
stories.summary: Tishman Speyer sold 400 Castro Street, a 138,000-square-foot Class A office building in downtown Mountain View, to Spear Street Capital for $121.5 million. The property, developed by Tishman Speyer in 2002, has remained 100% leased to anchor tenant Fenwick & West (a law firm) since initial delivery. Tishman Speyer claims the sale represents one of the strongest Mountain View office pricing outcomes in recent years.
stories.impact: CAUTIONARY SIGNAL FOR SILICON VALLEY MULTIFAMILY. Strong pricing on long-leased, single-tenant office (15%+ cap rate implied) suggests institutional capital is still willing to hold core office assets with strong, creditworthy anchors in Mountain View. However, this is an outlier; most Mountain View office is experiencing vacancy and downward pressure. For multifamily developers, this signals that tech-sector office employment remains concentrated but increasingly bifurcated—only trophy, fully-leased assets command premium pricing. Suburban and secondary office submarkets will see increased conversions, reducing white-collar job anchoring for residential demand in those areas. Focus multifamily growth on downtown cores (Palo Alto, Sunnyvale, San Jose) where office fundamentals remain stronger.

stories.title: Related Secures $65M Refi for Office Property in L.A.’s South Bay
stories.excerpt: The owners of a 301,000-square-foot Class A office property in Los Angeles’ South Bay have secured refinancing for the property. Owners Related Companies and Cruzan landed the $64.7 million loan from Waterfall Asset Management and Delaware Life for the eight-story property called the Torrance, named after its home city. The asset at 21250 Hawthorne Boulevard is 93 percent occupied, according to Yardi Matrix, with tenants including All Nippon Airways, Salon Republic, Barrister Executive Suites, Compass California, Unio Health Partners and Morgan Stanley. Newmark’s Jordan Roeschlaub, Nick Scribani and Chris Lozinak arranged the debt. The property was built in 1988. Related and Cruzan acquired it from Stream Realty Partners for $106.8 million in 2017, and secured $59.2 million in refinancing in 2022. The South Bay has benefited from surging demand from aerospace and defense users for both office and industrial space. But the Greater Los Angeles office market remains deeply bifurcated. Overall vacancy was at 25.3 percent after the second quarter, nearly unchanged from year-end 2025, while trophy properties have a 13.5 percent vacancy rate, according to Newmark research. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Related Companies and Cruzan refinanced Torrance (LA South Bay) office for $64.7M via Waterfall, Delaware Life.
301,000-sf Class A property (1988), 93% occupied; tenants include All Nippon Airways, Morgan Stanley.
South Bay demand driven by aerospace/defense users for office and industrial space.
stories.summary: Related Companies and Cruzan secured a $64.7 million refinancing from Waterfall Asset Management and Delaware Life for the Torrance, a 301,000-square-foot Class A office building in Los Angeles' South Bay. Built in 1988, the eight-story property is 93% occupied with tenants including All Nippon Airways, Morgan Stanley, and various professional services firms. The South Bay submarket has benefited from robust demand from aerospace and defense tenants for both office and industrial space.
stories.impact: POSITIVE DEMAND SIGNAL FOR LA SOUTH BAY MULTIFAMILY. Aerospace and defense sector strength (AeroVironment, Boeing, Northrop Grumman, SpaceX suppliers all active in region) is driving sustained office and industrial demand, which anchors blue-collar and professional-class employment. Strong office occupancy (93%) and successful refinancing on favorable terms signal lender confidence in South Bay employment durability. Multifamily developers should prioritize South Bay infill (Torrance, Manhattan Beach, Hermosa Beach, Redondo Beach) and Inland Empire warehouse-adjacent markets (aerospace supplier clustering), as aerospace/defense job growth and wage stability support rent growth more resilient to tech downturns than pure tech-dependent markets.
